body: What does this mean? It doesn't communicate to me at least what the reason is

Looking online this seems to be a word-for-word translation of a Polish idiom. I guess it can be replaced with something like "Must always be a Plane[6] array." I do love the constant threat of nasal demons though. It really sounds like something I don't want and will therefore ensure I always use a Plane[6]

It's something I've seen around (explained [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undefined_behavior)), and that I've been using as a funny but completely accurate way to refer to undefined behaviour.

> In the [C programming community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_(programming_language)), undefined behavior may be humorously referred to as "nasal demons", after a [comp.std.c](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comp.*_hierarchy) post that explained undefined behavior as allowing the compiler to do anything it chooses, even "to make demons fly out of your nose".

As for the actual reason for the comment: that struct is passed to functions that always expect the pointers to point at least to `Plane[6]` and `Vector3[8]`, which is the data required to represent a frustum. If the pointers points to something less than that, there's no bound checking, so you get undefined behaviour (hence nasal demons).

I thought about using vector, but when doing it this way I get to use stack arrays, saving some memory allocations during light setup. So I guess ultimately it boils down to slightly better performance and prettier if somewhat riskier code.

Then again, `DirectionalCullPlanes` is 1104 bytes...

Since that one time years back when I found out in my own code that MSVC *successfully* allows calling member functions on null pointers without crashing, despite this being undefined behaviour, I can't look at undefined behaviour the same anymore.

(of course that only worked because `this` wasn't being used in those functions, but still)
Using a stack array is definitely preferable in high performance code. The obscure reference to a comp.std.c post might not be as helpful though lol

Does this work as a demon-less version?

```cpp
const Plane *frustum_planes; // Functions expect this to store a frustum, so it must be ALWAYS at least Plane[6]. Undefined behaviour otherwise.
const Vector3 *frustum_points; // Functions expect this to store frustum corners, so it must be ALWAYS at least Vector3[8]. UB otherwise.
```

As said on RC, this is likely using an epsilon rather than zero to prevent numerical instability at extreme values, so it may be worth keeping an epsilon (unless it can be proven to work throughout the range with zero).

Yes, as far as I can see changes to the epsilons are not required for the cascade culling, and should be in the second epsilon PR.

We try to avoid unrelated changes in PRs for many reasons, including making tracking history difficult to follow, and make reverting etc more difficult in some cases.

Each PR should ideally be a single self contained change, that cannot be split any further. If something can be split into more than one logical independent unit, then ideally it should go in separate PRs.

There are some exceptions for major features, but that's normally the pattern for small changes.

This should ideally be explained in the contributor docs, I'll try and poke to get this added if it's not already there:
https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/pull_requests/pull_request_guidelines.html#contribute-one-change-at-a-time

See https://github.com/godotengine/godot-contributing-docs/pull/49 we are just adding some notes about this.
Renamed to `CullFrustumData`.

Isn't it kind of self-explanatory in this case? Godot only supports up to 4 cascades for directional lights.

Unless there is a public constant somewhere in the code that defines the maximum cascade count that can be used in place of this (I have no idea if there is).

`directional_cull_planes` was already there, I only added `camera_transform` and `camera_projection` for directional lights since there isn't yet any information about lights at the camera setup step, and without light information (cascade splits, max shadow distance) it's not possible to create proper cull planes for directional lights.

I have tested with the following scene (slot it into the MRP to test), and multi-light, multi-viewport setups seem to work fine.

[scene_multilight.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/24911378/scene_multilight.txt)

(the file is a `.tscn` file, just change the extension, GitHub wouldn't let me upload a bare `.tscn` file)

body: Reverted `_is_colinear_tri` to how it was before. That function is now more comments than code though :P

Yeah, it's likely fine here, and not something I personally would insist on if only used a couple of times.

A typical example of use is if in 5 years time no one knows what this code does, and they want to change to 5 cascades, they can just change a constant instead of having to read and understand the codebase here, to make sure e.g. they aren't writing to uninitialized memory or something.
Might be worth putting in a `default:` case here and `ERR_PRINT` or some error handling, so it becomes easy to identify problems if the enum is later changed?
There's also the code near `rendering_light_culler:137` that relies on constant max cascade count.
Yeah sometimes you can make them all depend on the same constant, but it's not a requirement to change from my side, just a good thing to aim for (I don't always do it myself :grin: ).
